ours.name: Sitkum Glacier
ours.approach: From the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (off Sloan Creek Road, FR 49), follow North Fork Sauk Trail #649 up the valley through old-growth forest, past the Red Creek bridge to Mackinaw Shelter, then up a long series of switchbacks to meet the Pacific Crest Trail at about 5,950 ft, roughly 8-9 miles from the car. White Pass and its camp are a short way south along the PCT; this route does not go there. Turn north on the PCT and cross Red Pass (about 6,500 ft) a mile or two on, then descend into the upper White Chuck valley and follow the PCT down it for roughly 7-9 miles, past the old White Chuck River Trail junction (~3,850 ft), to a forested campsite near 4,100 ft beside Sitkum Creek. fktText: Description summitpost.org : Glacier Peak (10,541') is one of the five volcanoes of the state of Washington, and is the highest mountain in Snohomish county. It has 7498 feet of prominence and ranks 5th highest on the Bulgar List (Washington Top 100) . It is located in the North Central part of the Cascades which it has a wilderness named after this mountain which is called the Glacier Peak Wilderness . The Native Americans once called this peak Takobia which would translate to "The Great Parent". This peak is classified as a stratovolcanoe (Composite) which there has not been any major activity in 300 years. This peak goes unnoticed by much of the people of the Northwest due to it being so far in the crest of the Cascades, its distance from the nearest town, and the fact that its access roads have been washed out making all the approaches to its base a long hike in. Glacier Peak can be seen from many locations along the Mountain Loop Highway , North Cascades , Highway 2 area, and many other high points through out the state. But this peak is often hidden from view from many low land areas which is another big reason it goes unnoticed by many. The summit offers amazing views of many of the great peaks of Washington, as well as a view of seeing far across the state. ours.name: Megalodon Ridge
ours.approach: Start at the Bridge Creek Trailhead on Highway 20 near milepost 159, just over a mile east of Rainy Pass (paved lot on the north side of the highway at about 4,400 ft), where a short connector trail crosses the highway to the Pacific Crest Trail, and head south on the PCT. Follow the PCT roughly 9-10 miles, descending along Bridge Creek, to the junction with the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail near North Fork Camp. Continue about 2 miles up this increasingly brushy trail along the North Fork of Bridge Creek and leave it at an obvious clearing before Grizzly Creek. fktText: Description At 9,199 feet, Goode is the tallest peak in the North Cascades and the eighth tallest peak in Washington State. Reached by crossing the Goode Glacier, the Northeast Buttress is a classic climbing route that features over 2,000 feet of mostly 3rd and 4th class climbing, with some 5th class mixed in. Most mountaineering parties complete the route in 2-3 days (the summit makes for a very nice bivy). The standard approach for the Northeast Buttress is via the Bridge Creek Trailhead on the North Cascades Highway (State Route 20). About 13 miles of flat and gradual downhill hiking brings you to an open area at the base of Goode. From here, it's about 5,800 feet of uphill gain to the summit. The descent is off the other side of the mountain, to the Park Creek Trail and back on the PCT at Bridge Creek—roughly 20 miles of well-maintained trail back to the Bridge Creek Trailhead. All told, this route includes about 33 miles of easy trail running (the majority on the PCT) and one large mountain climb. Goode can also be climbed from Stehekin, using a different approach to the same trail loop. ours.name: Northeast Face
ours.approach: South on Pacific Crest Trail along Bridge Creek for 9.6 miles to North Fork Bridge Creek Trail junction; then north with final bushwhacking to glacier base camp
ours.descent: The shared standard descent off Goode (used for this route as for the Northeast Buttress) is down the Southwest Couloir. From the summit ridge, downclimb/rappel a short sequence of stations to Black Tooth Notch — these first rappels trend more sideways/traversing than straight down, so expect some rope-snag risk and use care feeding rope; a single 60m rope is sufficient at every station. ours.name: Southwest Couloir
ours.approach: From the Bridge Creek/PCT trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 159 (just over a mile east of Rainy Pass, ~4,400 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail southbound along Bridge Creek. This stretch loses elevation steadily — roughly 1,600 ft over about 9.5-9.6 miles — down through forest to the North Fork Camp junction, where the PCT crosses Bridge Creek (a footbridge here has been washed out in past years; check current NPS conditions before counting on it). ours.name: Skyline Divide Route
ours.approach: From Glacier, WA, drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) east about 1 mile past the Glacier Public Service Center to Glacier Creek Road (FS 39); turn right, then take an immediate left onto Deadhorse Road (FS 37). FS 37 normally continues 12.7 miles to the Skyline Divide Trailhead. FS 37 has been closed by the 2021 flood washout at milepost 3.1, and during the repair work it is gated near its start (mile 0.03), so the trailhead is not reachable by vehicle; check the road's status before planning around it. When open, hike Skyline Divide Trail #678 through old-growth forest switchbacks and into meadows on the ridge crest (~2 mi), follow the crest to the trail's high point (~6,563 ft, ~4.5 mi), then
ours.descent: From the summit, carefully downclimb the short Class 3 step and the loose scree/talus below it back to the base of the summit block. Retrace the boot-packed path along Chowder Ridge and the open ridge crest (roughly 3 miles) back to the trail's high point (~6,563 ft), then descend the maintained Skyline Divide Trail #678 through meadows and forest switchbacks to the trailhead.

fktText: Description The elevation for Hadley Peak is at 7415. The route to Hadley Peak is through The Skyline Divide trail which is a 6000-foot-high ridgeline extension of Mount Baker. The Skyline Divide trail is 4.5 miles long before there is a 3 mile section that is a mix of boot pack path that runs the ridgeline over some of the most beautiful and magnificent terrain. As you approach the summit, there is a lot of loose rock and scree below the peak which makes the summit approach very difficult. At the peak there are views of Mount Baker and Mount Shuksan which are incredible. Total distance from trailhead to summit is 7.4 miles. ours.name: Inspiration Traverse
ours.approach: From the Eldorado Creek trailhead on the Cascade River Road, walk a short way down the road and cross the Cascade River on a log. A steep climbers' trail then gains roughly 1,800 ft through forest to a large boulder field around 4,000 ft. Cross the boulder field and Eldorado Creek into the open Eldorado Creek basin, climb to a notch on the ridge above, and drop into the Roush Creek basin at the foot of the Eldorado Glacier. Rope up and climb the Eldorado Glacier north to the broad, flat Inspiration Glacier, where the usual high camp sits on rock at the glacier's edge below Eldorado's East Ridge.
ours.descent: Reverse the approach: from the Klawatti col camp or the Inspiration Glacier high camp, cross back over the Inspiration Glacier, descend the Eldorado Glacier to the Roush Creek basin, climb back over the notch into the Eldorado Creek basin, then descend the boulder field and the steep forest trail to the Cascade River log crossing and the car. fktText: Description There are different interpretations of the famed " Inspiration Traverse " (depending of if you are climbing or ski'ing ) but upon reading multiple reports, for a car-to-car FKT style effort, the following is the most classic, desirable climber's line: Start from the Eldorado Trailhead and climb the 5 largest peaks of the traverse - Eldorado Peak (8,868') , Dorado Needle (8440') , Klawatti Peak (8485') , Austera Peak (8334') , and Primus Peak (8508') - before returning to the car. (an argument can be made for the point-to-point variation that exits out Thunder Creek, but the usual style for FKTs, especially considering the long car shuttle on this, is to do the car-to-car variations) the order the peaks are climbed is up to the FKT attempter. This is not a casual trail run . This route route has extensive crevassed glacier travel, steep snow, mid-5th class rock climbing, route finding, and exposed-high-risk terrain. Extensive experience with this skills is highly recommended before attempting. Planning for glacier conditions, weather, and day of the week (to avoid other parties) is a part of the logistics on this FKT. Be sure to read the route descriptions for the 4th/5th class terrain on Dorado, Klawatti, and Austera. You must tag the top of the true summit of each peak for this FKT to count...which on Dorado Needle includes a two move boulder problem that some describe as going at 5.7-5.9yds. ours.name: South Ridge
ours.approach: Start at the Denny Creek Trailhead (~2,280 ft), reached via Forest Road 58 (Denny Creek Road) off I-90 Exit 47. From the trailhead, follow Denny Creek Trail #1014 north/east up the valley. At roughly 1.2-1.3 miles the trail crosses Denny Creek at the 'Slippery Slab' — smooth cascading bedrock and pools that are the last easy, reliable water source before the climb steepens. Beyond the slab the trail climbs through forest, crosses talus/boulder slopes, and switchbacks up to Hemlock Pass (~3.8 miles, ~4,600 ft), where it meets the Melakwa Lake Trail #1011 junction (the right/east fork continues toward Lower Tuscohatchie Lake). ours.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line — the standard South Ridge route is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling. Downclimb the summit gully/ledge system carefully; loose, exfoliating rock is the primary hazard on the way down, so descend one climber at a time through the gully to avoid knocking rock onto partners below. fktText: Description Danny Naylor submitted the Route: Kaleetan Peak is an imposing rocky horn in the Snoqualmie Pass region of the central Cascade range. From the parking lot at the Denny Creek trailhead, off exit 47 of I-90, ascend the popular Denny Creek Trail to Melakwa Lake. Cross the lake's outlet stream and follow a climber's bootpack up the ridge to your left (west side of the lake). Follow this unmaintained trail over the first major prominence as it drops partially down onto the western slope of the ridge and across a talus field before turning back uphill for the final push to the summit. The climber's trail requires comfort on talus, and the final summit gully is a (relatively easy) class 3 scramble. This route is approximately 5.5 miles each way with a net elevation difference of over 3,900' between trailhead and summit. ours.approach: From I-90 Exit 52 (West Snoqualmie Pass), the Pacific Crest Trailhead (PCT northbound) lot sits just off the exit ramp on a short dirt spur (Northwest Forest Pass required; the ~50-car lot fills early on weekends). From the trailhead (~3,000 ft), follow the PCT north through second-growth forest: a first switchback at 0.6 mi (3,230 ft), a switchback pair at 1.5 mi (3,690 ft), and the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary at 2.0 mi (3,830 ft), where the forest opens into talus. The trail eases downhill slightly to the Commonwealth Creek Trail junction at 2.6 mi (3,775 ft) - stay right/straight on the PCT; the left-hand Commonwealth Basin trail is brushy and easy to mistake for the main tread. fktText: Description This aesthetic, non-techincal, off trail route traverses the highest, most rugged terrain of the central Alpine Lakes Wilderness. It is comparable to the famous Ptarmigan Traverse in the North Cascades, but is slightly longer, more rugged, and much less traveled. It starts on the PCT from Snoqualmie Pass, ascends over Chikamin Peak, down to Iceberg Lake, up to Overcoat Glacier, across to Summit Chief Pass, to Williams Lake, up to La Bohn Gap, over the summit of Hinman, to Pea Soup Lake, and over Mt. Daniel to the Cathedral Pass Trailhead. It totals to about 37 miles and 14-15k ft gain. A full trip report (with MANY photos) can be found at: https://climberkyle.com/2019/06/30/the-alpine-lakes-crest-traverse/ . fktText: Description Chikamin Peak is the first Cascade mountain north of Mount Rainier to reach over 7000 feet in elevation, and an excellent destination for a day trip. This route follows the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT) north from Snoqualmie Pass, requires a short scramble up the south side of Chikamin Peak, and then reconnects back to the PCT via Chikamin and Glacier lakes. The same route was also previously described by Climber Kyle . ours.name: Southwest Slope - Southeast Ridge
ours.approach: From the White River Trailhead (~2,300 ft) follow the White River Trail and Boulder Creek to a ford/camp around 3,700 ft, then continue up into Boulder Basin to a high camp near 5,800 ft. From high camp, traverse via Clark Basin and Luahna Basin (crossing a faint sheepherder's trail with significant side-hilling) to reach the base of Luahna's southwest slope.
ours.descent: From the summit, downclimb the class 3 section, re-cross the exposed class 3+ traverse beneath the summit, and descend the class 2 south-face ledges back to the ridge and basin below. From there retrace the sheepherder's-trail traverse back through Luahna, Clark, and Boulder basins to the high camp, then follow Boulder Creek and the White River Trail back to the trailhead.

fktText: Description CLARK MOUNTAIN - 8602' and LUAHNA PEAK - 8400' are commonly climbed together by mountaineers and peakbagging enthusiasts alike, with both a glaciated route requiring roped travel and an alternative traverse avoiding the glaciers. This is not a casual trail run, technical mountain skills, including glacier travel, rope skills, crampon use, and ice axe use are necessary. The following adapted from The Mountaineers: GETTING THERE Drive US 2 (Stevens Pass Highway) to the Lake Wenatchee turn-off (Coles Corner, 20.3 mi east of Stevens Pass). Turn north on Lake Wenatchee River Road (SR 207); bear left after crossing the Wenatchee River, proceeding west along the north shore of the lake passing the Lake Wenatchee Ranger Station. About 1.5 mi after the ranger station, take the right fork—White River Road (Forest Road 6400), to the end of the road (about 11 mi). APPROACH Travel the mainly level and easy White River Trail 4 mi to the junction with Boulder Creek Trail (.25 mi past the bridge over Boulder Creek). Ascend Boulder Creek trail. At 4,000 ft, the trail crosses Boulder Creek. Either wade the creek or use small tree. Continue up trail to suggested campsite at edge of clearing in large open basin at 4,900 ft (7.5 mi). There is an alternate base camp at 6,000 ft (8.5 mi), just below Boulder Pass. ASCENT ROUTE CLARK MOUNTAIN/WALRUS GLACIER Find Boulder Pass Trail north of campsite and ascend toward Boulder Pass.
